entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10115"/><div sID="gen18042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10115"/><hi type="bold">2. figs ... first ripe--</hi>the "boccora," or early fig (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.28.4">Is 28:4</reference>). Baskets of figs used to be offered as first-fruits in the temple. The good figs represent Jeconiah and the exiles in Babylon; the bad, Zedekiah and the obstinate Jews in Judea. They are called good and bad respectively, not in an absolute, but a comparative sense, and in reference to the punishment of the latter. This prophecy was designed to encourage the despairing exiles, and to reprove the people at home, who prided themselves as superior to those in Babylon and abused the forbearance of God (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.52.31-Jer.52.34">Jr 52:31-34</reference>). <div eID="gen18042" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10118"/><div sID="gen18047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10118"/>7. (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.22">Jr 30:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.33">31:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.38">32:38</reference>). Their conversion from idolatry to the one true God, through the chastening effect of the Babylonish captivity, is here expressed in language which, in its fulness, applies to the more complete conversion hereafter of the Jews, "with their whole heart" (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.13">Jr 29:13</reference>), through the painful discipline of their present dispersion. The source of their conversion is here stated to be God's prevenient grace.<div eID="gen18047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for they shall return--</hi>Repentance, though not the cause of pardon, is its invariable accompaniment: it is the effect of God's giving a heart to know Him. <div eID="gen18048" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 7. ( Jr 30:22 ; 31:33 ; 32:38 ). Their conversion from idolatry to the one true God, through the chastening effect of the Babylonish captivity, is here expressed in language which, in its fulness, applies to the more complete conversion hereafter of the Jews, "with their whole heart" ( Jr 29:13 ), through the painful discipline of their present dispersion. The source of their conversion is here stated to be God's prevenient grace. for they shall return-- Repentance, though not the cause of pardon, is its invariable accompaniment: it is the effect of God's giving a heart to know Him.
